$comment: Where 'true in general' and 'safe as done by a child in a kitchen' come apart. A caution is attached to a hazard, not restated per item, so the wording stays consistent across the whole chain. The game explains how these things work; it is not a method, and the wording must never imply otherwise.

botulism.label: Preserving is not a recipe you can eyeball
botulism.note: Fermenting and curing at home is real food science and it has a real failure mode. Clostridium botulinum grows in exactly the conditions these methods create — low oxygen, low acid, room temperature — and the toxin has no taste or smell. Salt concentration, acidity and temperature are not details; they are the whole safety margin. Follow a tested method from a food-safety authority, not a game.

caustic.label: Lye burns on contact
caustic.note: Sodium hydroxide is strongly caustic. It damages skin and eyes immediately and generates heat when it meets water. Historic soap-making is a good story and a bad first experiment.

fire.label: Fire and hot fat
fire.note: Cooking oil reaches temperatures that ignite, and water thrown into it will throw burning oil across a room. Never leave hot fat unattended, and never put water on an oil fire.

raw.label: Raw egg and unpasteurised milk
raw.note: Both can carry salmonella or listeria. The risk is small for most people and much larger if you are pregnant, very young, elderly, or immunocompromised.

alcohol.label: Alcohol
alcohol.note: Fermentation is how alcohol is made, and this part of the game explains that chemistry. It is not a brewing guide, and the drinking age where you live applies to you and not to the game.

cherry_kernel.label: The stone, not the fruit
cherry_kernel.note: Cherry flesh is entirely safe and this caution is not about eating cherries. The kernels inside the hard pits contain amygdalin, which releases hydrogen cyanide when chewed or swallowed. Do not crack the stones open.

mercury_toxicity.label: Mercury is toxic, in the ore and in the metal
mercury_toxicity.note: Mercury and its compounds are toxic to the nervous system, immune system and kidneys, and both mining cinnabar and refining mercury from it are historic causes of mercury poisoning. This is chemistry to understand, not something to try at home.

uranium_toxicity.label: Uranium is a heavy-metal poison first
uranium_toxicity.note: The main risk of exposure is chemical poisoning by uranium oxide rather than radioactivity — incorporated uranium accumulates in bone, liver, kidney and reproductive tissue. An excess risk of lung cancer has been documented among Navajo uranium miners specifically and linked to their occupation.

reactive_metal.label: These metals set fire to water
reactive_metal.note: Sodium forms flammable hydrogen and caustic sodium hydroxide on contact with water, and potassium reacts hard enough to ignite that hydrogen itself. Magnesium burns at around 3,100°C with a brilliant white light carrying strong ultraviolet. This is real chemistry, and none of it is a demonstration to improvise.

lead_toxicity.label: Lead is a neurotoxin
lead_toxicity.note: Lead is a neurotoxin that accumulates in soft tissue and bone. It damages the nervous system, interferes with biological enzymes, and can cause neurological problems ranging from behavioural issues to brain damage.

chlorine_gas.label: Chlorine gas is a poison, and was used as one
chlorine_gas.note: Elemental chlorine at high concentration is extremely dangerous and poisonous to most living organisms. It was the first gas deployed as a weapon, at the Second Battle of Ypres on 22 April 1915. This page is about where an industrial chemical comes from, and nothing on it is a method.

fluorine_hazard.label: Fluorine is why chemistry has martyrs
fluorine_hazard.note: Fluorine in its elemental form is highly toxic, and it reacts with almost every other element. Several nineteenth-century experimenters who tried to isolate it were injured or killed, and are remembered as the fluorine martyrs.

arsenic_toxicity.label: Arsenic is a poison, and a drinking-water problem
arsenic_toxicity.note: Arsenic compounds have been known since ancient times to be poisonous. The commonest cause of long-term exposure today is not deliberate — it is contaminated groundwater, and more than 200 million people worldwide are exposed to unsafe levels.

selenium_dose.label: Essential and toxic are the same element, at different doses
selenium_dose.note: Selenium is a required nutrient: the adult recommended intake is 55 micrograms a day and the tolerable upper limit is 400. Exceeding it causes selenosis. That is a narrow window compared with almost anything else on the shelf.

heavy_metal_dust.label: Some metals are only dangerous once they are dust
heavy_metal_dust.note: Cadmium is toxic and accumulates in the kidneys. Manganese overexposure causes manganism, a permanent movement disorder. Osmium tetroxide, which forms when osmium powder meets air, damages eyes and lungs at very low concentrations.

radioactivity.label: These are radioactive, and that is the point of some of them
radioactivity.note: Radium, thorium, plutonium and polonium are all radioactive. Radium was painted onto watch dials by women who wet the brushes with their lips, and many of them died of it — the Radium Girls case changed occupational-safety law. Polonium is acutely toxic in microgram amounts.

calcium_corrosive.label: Calcium metal burns skin on contact
calcium_corrosive.note: Calcium reacts with water faster than magnesium does, giving calcium hydroxide and hydrogen. Because that reaction is exothermic, calcium metal touching the moisture on skin causes severe corrosive irritation, and swallowing it does the same to the mouth, oesophagus and stomach.

lightning.label: Thunder is the sound of something already close
lightning.note: A lightning channel carries current through air heated to tens of thousands of degrees, and a strike does not have to hit a person to injure one — current spreads outward through the ground and through anything that conducts. Thunder is that channel being heard, so hearing it means the storm is already within range of it.

severe_weather.label: Weather that kills people
severe_weather.note: Flood, storm surge, hurricane, blizzard and large hail are in this game because they are real physics, and they are the parts of that physics that kill. Moving floodwater carries and hides things and is far stronger than it looks; a blizzard removes visibility rather than merely reducing it; storm surge is the sea being pushed onto land.

ozone.label: Ozone is not fresh air
ozone.note: The clean smell after a thunderstorm is a toxic gas. The same oxidising power that makes ozone useful for disinfecting is what damages mucous and respiratory tissue in animals, and plant tissue too, above about 0.1 ppm — around the level that already produces headaches and burning eyes.

methanol_toxicity.label: Methanol looks and smells like drinking alcohol
methanol_toxicity.note: It is difficult to tell methanol, ethanol and isopropyl alcohol apart by appearance or odour, and methanol is far more acutely toxic. The body turns it into formaldehyde and then formate, which shuts down the enzyme cells use to breathe. As little as 4 to 15 mL has reportedly caused irreversible optic nerve damage.

phenol_corrosive.label: Phenol degrades protein on contact
phenol_corrosive.note: Its corrosive effect on skin and mucous membrane comes from degenerating the protein itself, and prolonged contact can produce second and third-degree burns. It also passes into the blood through unbroken skin, and systemic poisoning can follow within minutes to hours.

formaldehyde_carcinogen.label: Formaldehyde is a carcinogen, not just a smell
formaldehyde_carcinogen.note: The International Agency for Research on Cancer reclassified formaldehyde as a known human carcinogen, associated with nasal sinus and nasopharyngeal cancer. Above about 0.1 ppm in air it irritates the eyes and mucous membranes. It is also what makes smoke-tanned hide keep, and what hardened the first casein plastics.

venomous_spur.label: The platypus is a venomous mammal
venomous_spur.note: The male carries a spur on each hind leg fed by a gland in the thigh, and the venom is powerful enough to inflict pain in humans — swelling, and a heightened sensitivity to pain that can last as long as months. It is largely defensin-like proteins, some of them unique to the species, and the spurs are weapons males use on each other.

lion_predation.label: Man-eating is a supplement, not a last resort
lion_predation.note: The Tsavo pair stopped the Uganda Railway in 1898; Patterson claimed 135 victims and a later review of his journal put it nearer 28–31. The modern figure is larger and less famous: more than 563 people killed in Tanzania since 1990 and at least 308 injured, with attacks peaking at harvest time. Studies of man-eating lions find that African lions eat people as a supplement to other food rather than because they are starving.

bear_defence.label: A defensive animal, not a predatory one
bear_defence.note: Brown bears seldom attack on sight and usually avoid people. What changes that is surprise or a threat to cubs: sows with cubs account for the majority of injuries and fatalities in North America. That is a different mechanism from a hunting animal, and it is why the danger is a function of distance and warning rather than of hunger.

rattlesnake_bite.label: A real venom, and a real treatment for it
rattlesnake_bite.note: About seven to eight thousand people are bitten by venomous snakes in the United States each year, and up to 95% of the snakebite deaths there are attributed to western and eastern diamondback rattlesnakes specifically. Antivenom, given intravenously, is effective at preventing death — but it works by binding and neutralising the venom enzymes already in the body, and it carries its own side effects. It is a hospital treatment, not a home one.

elephant_musth.label: A herbivore, dangerous for a reason that has nothing to do with diet
elephant_musth.note: Adult bulls enter a periodic state of raised testosterone called musth, marked by a fluid running from the temporal gland down the side of the face. Males become extremely aggressive during it, and working elephants in musth are chained until it passes. Human–elephant conflict kills as many as 80 people a year in Sri Lanka, where farmers kill more than 230 elephants in return.

road_animal.label: The dangerous ones are the ones you meet at speed
road_animal.note: Deer-vehicle collisions run to 500,000 a year in Europe and 1–1.5 million in North America, and together account for some 30,000 injuries and 200 deaths. Nine out of ten animal collisions in Australia involve kangaroos, which cross at around 50 km/h and are heavy enough to come through a windscreen. By comparison only two fatal kangaroo attacks have ever been reliably documented in Australia.

sting_anaphylaxis.label: The sting is a protein, and the reaction is an allergy
sting_anaphylaxis.note: Most stings produce a local reaction. An estimated 5–10% of people have a generalised systemic response instead, and in the United States about 40 people a year die of anaphylaxis from stinging-insect allergy. The mechanism is the same IgE pathway as a food allergy — a venom protein where a seed protein would be — which is why an insect sting and a peanut appear in the same part of a medical textbook.

thujone_toxicity.label: Thujone in concentrated sage oil
thujone_toxicity.note: Ordinary cooking with sage leaves is not the concern here. Sage essential oil contains α- and β-thujone, a neurotoxin that can cause convulsions in animals and severe intoxication in humans, which is why European regulators cap supplemental use at 6 mg a day. The leaf on a plate and the oil in a bottle are not the same dose.

bay_leaf_hazard.label: Bay leaves are for flavour, not for eating
bay_leaf_hazard.note: Bay leaves stay stiff even after long cooking and can pose a choking hazard or abrade the digestive tract if swallowed whole. They are meant to flavour a dish and be lifted back out before serving, never eaten.

niacin_flush.label: Niacin flush is a real, dose-triggered reaction
niacin_flush.note: Ordinary dietary niacin is not the concern here. More than 30 mg taken as a supplement can flush the face, arms and chest — vasodilation from a spike in prostaglandin and serotonin, usually gone in 15 to 30 minutes. Sustained-release niacin at medicinal doses (500 to 3,000 mg a day) carries a real risk of liver damage.

b6_neuropathy.label: Vitamin B6 neuropathy is a supplement-dose problem
b6_neuropathy.note: Ordinary dietary B6 is not the concern. Above roughly 1,000 mg a day, taken as a supplement over a long period, pyridoxine causes a painful, sometimes irreversible nerve damage — pain and numbness in the hands and feet, and in severe cases trouble walking. Regulators disagree sharply on where the safe ceiling is: the EU sets 12 mg a day, the US 100.

vitamin_e_bleeding.label: Vitamin E can potentiate blood thinners
vitamin_e_bleeding.note: Vitamin E from food is not the concern. Supplemental doses above roughly 300 mg a day can increase the anti-clotting action of aspirin, warfarin and other blood thinners, and the US upper intake limit of 1,000 mg a day was set from bleeding risk observed in animal studies.

eu_dye_hyperactivity_warning.label: The EU requires a warning label on this dye
eu_dye_hyperactivity_warning.note: Red 40, Yellow 5 and Yellow 6 are three of the 'Southampton Six' synthetic dyes an EU regulation, effective 2010, requires be labelled 'may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children.' The underlying science is genuinely disputed: some studies link the dyes to hyperactivity in children, others do not, and the EU and US regulators have reached different conclusions from the same evidence.

yellow_5_allergy_warning.label: Yellow 5 carries its own FDA-mandated allergy warning
yellow_5_allergy_warning.note: The US FDA requires products containing tartrazine to state that it may cause allergic-type reactions, including bronchial asthma, in certain susceptible people — a separate concern from the EU attention warning above, and specific to Yellow 5 among the four dyes in this batch.

blue_1_enteral_advisory.label: A 2003 FDA advisory, and it is not about candy
blue_1_enteral_advisory.note: Ordinary food and drink use is not what this is about. In 2003 the FDA warned health care providers specifically about this dye's potential toxicity when used to tint enteral (feeding-tube) nutrition solutions, after reports of patient harm in that clinical context.

shiitake_dermatitis.label: Raw shiitake can cause a rash
shiitake_dermatitis.note: Rarely, eating shiitake raw or only lightly cooked triggers 'shiitake dermatitis' — a streaky, itchy rash that appears about 24 hours later, covering much of the body including the face and scalp. Cooking it through is the difference.

spirulina_contamination.label: Spirulina supplements and contamination
spirulina_contamination.note: Spirulina itself doesn't make toxins. But some supplements have tested positive for microcystins from co-occurring toxic blue-green algae, and China's food safety regulator found lead, mercury and arsenic widespread in spirulina supplements sold there. The organism is not the hazard; unregulated sourcing is.

synephrine_cardio.label: Synephrine carries ephedra's risk profile, not a safer one
synephrine_cardio.note: Marketed as the ephedra-free stimulant after ephedra was banned, bitter orange is believed to cause the same spectrum of adverse events. Case reports link it to stroke, myocardial infarction and angina; the NCCIH found little evidence it is actually safer.

caffeine_powder.label: Caffeine from coffee or tea is not the same risk as the pure powder
caffeine_powder.note: Caffeine from coffee or tea is not the concern here — the FDA still calls it generally recognized as safe, and a lethal dose that way is something like 75 to 100 cups. Pure powdered caffeine sold as a supplement is different: a level tablespoon can be a lethal dose, and it has killed people who measured by volume instead of a scale.

horsetail_thiaminase.label: Horsetail's thiaminase, over time
horsetail_thiaminase.note: Field horsetail contains thiaminase, an enzyme that breaks down vitamin B1. It is documented as toxic to livestock, particularly horses, when eaten over a long enough period — a dose-over-time problem, not an instant one.

aloin_laxative.label: Aloe's outer leaf layer is not the gel
aloin_laxative.note: Aloe vera's gel core is one thing; the outer leaf layer holds aloin, a bitter latex compound the FDA banned from over-the-counter laxatives in 2002. Oral ingestion of aloe extracts can cause abdominal pain, cramps, and hepatitis if taken chronically.

psyllium_choking.label: Psyllium needs water to go with it
psyllium_choking.note: Psyllium husk swells into mucilage on contact with liquid. Taken without enough water it can thicken in the throat and become a choking hazard, or form a bowel obstruction or bezoar further down.

fos_fodmap.label: FOS is a FODMAP
fos_fodmap.note: Fructooligosaccharides resist human digestive enzymes and are fermented by bacteria in the colon instead, producing gas. That fermentation is well tolerated by most people at ordinary doses, but not by people with Irritable Bowel Syndrome or FODMAP sensitivity.

ginseng_interactions.label: Ginseng interacts with medication
ginseng_interactions.note: Panax ginseng is generally considered safe for adults used under six months, but it can interact with prescription drugs such as warfarin, and its use during pregnancy and breastfeeding is considered potentially unsafe.

salmonella_illness.label: Salmonella causes real food poisoning
salmonella_illness.note: Nontyphoidal Salmonella infection generally causes gastroenteritis — food poisoning, in plain terms — and the US alone counts about 1,200,000 cases a year. Most healthy adults recover without incident; infants, the elderly, organ-transplant recipients and anyone immunocompromised are the ones genuinely at risk of it turning severe.

aspirin_reye.label: Reye syndrome links aspirin to a rare, severe childhood illness
aspirin_reye.note: About 90% of Reye syndrome cases in children are associated with aspirin (salicylate) use during a viral illness, which is why health guidance in the United States says aspirin should not be given to anyone under 19 during a fever-causing illness. The syndrome itself is rare — under one in a million children a year — but death occurs in 20 to 40% of those affected, and about a third of survivors are left with lasting brain damage.

streptomycin_ototoxicity.label: Streptomycin can cause permanent hearing and balance damage
streptomycin_ototoxicity.note: Like other aminoglycoside antibiotics, streptomycin's most concerning side effects are kidney and ear toxicity. Damage to the vestibulocochlear nerve can be transient or permanent, causing tinnitus, vertigo, loss of balance, or deafness — and use during pregnancy has been linked to permanent congenital deafness in the child.

insulin_hypoglycemia.label: Too much insulin is a medical emergency, not a dosing error to shrug off
insulin_hypoglycemia.note: Insulin in excess of what the body needs to handle the carbohydrate it has eaten causes hypoglycemic coma and can kill. Symptoms include dizziness, weakness, trembling, seizures, confusion and drowsiness, escalating to coma.

penicillin_allergy.label: Penicillin allergy is common to claim, rare to confirm
penicillin_allergy.note: About 10% of people in the United States report a penicillin allergy, but the great majority were never truly allergic or have outgrown it — skin-test positivity drops by about 10% with every year of avoidance, and roughly 90% of self-reported cases can eventually tolerate penicillin again. A true IgE-mediated anaphylactic reaction is rare, occurring in roughly 0.01% of patients, though a milder rash affects 1 to 10%.

apricot_kernel.label: The kernel, not the flesh
apricot_kernel.note: Apricot flesh is entirely safe and this caution is not about eating apricots. The kernel inside the pit contains amygdalin — bitter kernels run about 5% amygdalin, sweet ones about 0.9% — which breaks down into cyanide. Do not eat the kernel.

rhubarb_leaf.label: The stalk, not the leaf
rhubarb_leaf.note: Rhubarb's stalk is what's eaten. The leaf blade contains oxalic acid, a nephrotoxin, and real poisonings have followed eating the leaves — including a wartime shortage-era recommendation in Britain that was later withdrawn.

bean_lectin.label: Raw beans are not a recipe you can eyeball
bean_lectin.note: Raw or undercooked common beans contain phytohaemagglutinin, a toxic lectin — most concentrated in red kidney beans, but present across the species. A full rolling boil for at least 30 minutes destroys it; a slow cooker's lower heat does not.

cashew_shell.label: The shell is a poison-ivy relative
cashew_shell.note: Raw cashew shells and unroasted seeds carry anacardic acid, a potent skin-irritant resin chemically related to the toxin in poison ivy. Commercial cashews are always shelled and roasted or steamed before sale for exactly this reason.

cassia_coumarin.label: Cassia cinnamon carries far more coumarin than Ceylon
cassia_coumarin.note: Cassia cinnamon — the common supermarket kind — runs well over 1mg of coumarin per gram, sometimes far more; true Ceylon cinnamon carries only trace amounts. High coumarin intake over time risks liver and kidney harm.

nutmeg_myristicin.label: Nutmeg's own toxin, in excess
nutmeg_myristicin.note: Myristicin, nutmeg's own compound, is a toxin in pure form — consuming excessive amounts of nutmeg can cause real myristicin poisoning, not just an upset stomach.

ecoli_illness.label: E. coli is usually harmless, and sometimes isn't
ecoli_illness.note: Most E. coli strains are part of the normal gut microbiota and are harmless or even beneficial. Pathogenic strains are a different matter: some cause serious food poisoning, and virulent strains can cause gastroenteritis, urinary tract infections, neonatal meningitis, and hemorrhagic colitis.

paracetamol_overdose.label: Paracetamol overdose is a leading cause of acute liver failure
paracetamol_overdose.note: Paracetamol is safe at the recommended dose and dangerous well before it tastes dangerous. Taking more than the maximum adult daily dose — three to four grams — can cause potentially fatal liver damage. Paracetamol toxicity is one of the leading causes of poisoning in high-income countries, and the single most common cause of acute liver failure in many of them.

cowpox_zoonosis.label: Cowpox still circulates — now mostly by way of cats
cowpox_zoonosis.note: Despite the name, cowpox's usual wild hosts are woodland rodents, particularly voles, not cattle. Domestic cats catch it from those rodents and can pass it on to their owners, which is how most human cowpox cases happen today.

histamine_scombroid.label: Histamine is also a real fish-poisoning toxin
histamine_scombroid.note: Above about 16°C, bacteria on improperly stored fish convert the histidine already in the flesh into histamine, and enough of it causes scombroid food poisoning: flushed skin, headache, itching and cramps, usually from tuna, mackerel or other dark-fleshed fish left too warm for too long.

shark_bite.label: Rare, but the numbers are real
shark_bite.note: Unprovoked bites are uncommon set against how many people swim in shark habitat, but they are documented: 351 unprovoked great white bites since 1580, 59 of them fatal, and the tiger shark ranks second worldwide for fatal attacks. Bull sharks are one of the three species most often implicated in bites on people, and oceanic whitetips were blamed for attacks on shipwreck survivors as recently as the 1945 sinking of the USS Indianapolis.

blue_ringed_octopus_bite.label: No antivenom exists for this bite
blue_ringed_octopus_bite.note: The bite itself is often painless, and the octopus is docile — there are no reported cases of it attacking a person unprovoked. But the tetrodotoxin it carries blocks nerve signal at the source, and without artificial respiration started fast enough a serious bite can be fatal within hours. There is no antivenom; the only treatment is life support until the toxin clears the body on its own.

box_jellyfish_sting.label: The most venomous animal most people never see
box_jellyfish_sting.note: Chironex fleckeri, the largest box jellyfish species, has caused at least 79 recorded deaths since 1883, and a severe sting can bring on cardiac arrest within two minutes. Most encounters with box jellyfish are far milder than that worst case, but the ones that are not do not leave time to look up a treatment.

venomous_fish_sting.label: A real venom, and a real treatment for it
venomous_fish_sting.note: Stonefish carry the most potent venom of any fish known — stings have caused documented deaths in Australia and Japan, and stonefish antivenom is the second most-administered antivenom in Australia. Lionfish deliver a milder but genuine venom through long dorsal spines; it rarely kills a healthy adult but has killed young children, the elderly, and people allergic to it. For both, hot water above 45°C denatures the venom and is the standard field first aid, alongside proper medical care.

piranha_bite.label: Rare, and rarely serious — but real
piranha_bite.note: The pack-hunter reputation is mostly myth, and unprovoked attacks on people are uncommon. But piranhas do bite: incidents at crowded swimming spots in Brazil and Argentina have sent dozens of people to hospital with foot and heel wounds in a single day, mostly minor, occasionally needing stitches. Fatal attacks are exceptionally rare.

scorpion_sting.label: Real venom, and it varies a lot by species
scorpion_sting.note: Most scorpion stings cause pain and swelling and nothing worse. A handful of genera in the family Buthidae are the exception — Androctonus and Leiurus in North Africa and the Middle East, Centruroides in Mexico, Tityus in South America — with venom that can be medically serious. Scorpion stings are estimated to cause around 3,000 deaths a year worldwide, concentrated in the regions those genera live.

tick_borne_disease.label: A real disease risk, tied to how long it feeds
tick_borne_disease.note: Ixodes ticks are the main carrier of Lyme disease, and transmission risk rises sharply the longer a tick stays attached to its host, with most studies putting the threshold around 24 hours. Even so, only an estimated 1.2 to 1.4% of recognised tick bites result in Lyme disease, and people treated with antibiotics within days of the first symptoms have the best outcomes.

$severity: How loudly to say it. acute: can kill or permanently injure. contact: burns, corrodes or envenomates on contact. cumulative: harms with exposure over time. conditional: harms only some people, or only in some circumstances. The tier decides the signal on the card; it is never a ranking of how bad a thing is, and it is never advice.
